**A Soldier's Play** represents a significant theatrical milestone, bringing Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama to Broadway for the first time in a revival that critics find both powerful and timely. Two reimagined classics also stand out: **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club** transforms the August Wilson Theatre into an immersive nightclub experience, with Rebecca Frecknall's bold direction earning widespread acclaim, while Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped **Company** breathes new life into Sondheim's masterwork with Katrina Lenk stepping into the traditionally male lead role.

With an average critic score of 81/100 across these ten productions, the 2021 season showcases both artistic ambition and theatrical craftsmanship. Whether you're drawn to experimental storytelling or classic spectacle, these shows offer compelling reasons to experience live theater.

Leading our rankings is **Les Misérables** (83/100), a grittier reboot at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre that reimagines the beloved musical with a darker, more visceral approach. While some traditionalists remain unconvinced, most critics praise the production's bold reinvention.

**A Soldier's Play** (78/100) stands as another highlight—Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama finally received its long-overdue Broadway debut in a stellar revival. The production demonstrates how this examination of racism and power within a World War II-era Black regiment remains urgently relevant, earning widespread critical acclaim across 29 reviews.

The remaining shows in our top five present more divided critical responses. **My Name is Lucy Barton** (71/100) showcases Laura Linney's luminous solo performance in an adaptation of Elizabeth Strout's novel, though critics split on the material itself. **Grand Horizons** (71/100) offers boulevard comedy elevated by Jane Alexander's performance, while **West Side Story** (68/100) features Ivo van Hove's radical reimagining that polarizes audiences with its bold departures from tradition.

With an average critic score of 74/100 across these five productions, the 2020 season—though brief—delivered substantive theatrical experiences ranging from intimate character studies to ambitious reinterpretations of classics. Explore our detailed reviews below to discover which of these productions align with your theatrical tastes.

# Best Broadway Plays That Opened in 2021

As Broadway looks back from March 2026, the 2021 season stands as a watershed moment—the year live theater roared back to life after the pandemic shutdown. What emerged was not just a return to normalcy, but a season of remarkable artistic ambition and innovation that continues to resonate with audiences today.

The ten productions featured here average an impressive 81/100 critical score, reflecting a year when Broadway took meaningful creative risks. Leading the pack is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama that earns widespread acclaim for Deirdre O'Connell's mesmerizing lip-sync performance to her real mother's interview recordings—a theatrical experiment that critics call both unsettling and unforgettable.

The season balanced experimental work with spectacular revials. Rebecca Frecknall's **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club** transforms the August Wilson Theatre into an immersive nightclub experience that critics praise as revelatory, while Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped **Company** breathes new life into Sondheim's masterwork with Katrina Lenk in the central role. Meanwhile, Sam Mendes' epic staging of **The Lehman Trilogy** chronicles 150 years of American capitalism through extraordinary performances and stunning stagecraft.

The 2021 season also marked historic firsts: Antoinette Chinonye Nwandu's **Pass Over** became the first play to reopen Broadway, setting a tone of urgency and purpose. Intimate productions like **Is This a Room** and **Lackawanna Blues** proved that small-scale storytelling could command Broadway stages alongside mega-musicals like **The Phantom of the Opera** and the pop-fueled **SIX**.

Whether you're discovering these productions for the first time or revisiting the season that saved Broadway, these ten shows represent theater at its most vital and varied.

Jackson's Pulitzer-winning meta-musical—earns widespread acclaim for its brazenly original and brutally honest exploration of Black queer identity.

What distinguishes this collection is its concentration of Pulitzer Prize-winning works, including Suzan-Lori Parks' *Topdog/Underdog*, Tom Stoppard's deeply personal *Leopoldstadt*, and Paula Vogel's *How I Learned to Drive*. These acclaimed dramas sit alongside innovative comedies like Mike Birbiglia's *The Old Man & The Pool* and audacious satires such as *Ain't No Mo'*, demonstrating the breadth of theatrical storytelling that defined the season.

The 2022 season proves particularly notable for giving voice to previously underrepresented perspectives while honoring theatrical masters, creating a landscape where experimental new works and carefully crafted revivals coexist and elevate one another. Whether these shows remain running or have completed their Broadway engagements, they represent essential viewing for anyone seeking to understand contemporary American theater at its finest.

best-broadway-plays-2023.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2023

As of March 2026, the exceptional class of plays that opened on Broadway in 2023 continues to demonstrate the enduring power of dramatic storytelling on the New York stage. With an impressive average critic score of 82/100 across our featured productions, this cohort represents one of the strongest years for non-musical theatre in recent memory.

Leading the field is Maria Friedman's acclaimed revival of **Merrily We Roll Along**, which stands as a testament to how thoughtful reinterpretation can transform even Sondheim's most challenging works into theatrical triumphs. Close behind, **Stranger Things: The First Shadow** proves that intellectual property adaptations can transcend their source material when executed with technical brilliance and dramatic ambition, while **Appropriate** has established itself as essential contemporary American drama, with Sarah Paulson anchoring a searing family narrative that critics have embraced as a modern masterpiece.

The year's offerings span remarkable range—from the timely urgency of **Parade** and the long-overdue revival of **Purlie Victorious** to Alex Edelman's solo tour de force **Just for Us** and the Pulitzer-winning **Fat Ham**. Traditional revivals like **Sweeney Todd** share the spotlight with innovative new works like **Stereophonic**, demonstrating Broadway's capacity to honor its heritage while pushing theatrical boundaries.

This collection of ten productions showcases theatre at its most vital: politically engaged, emotionally resonant, and artistically ambitious. Whether you're drawn to classic revivals reimagined for contemporary audiences or bold new voices reshaping American drama, these shows offer compelling reasons to experience live theatre at its finest.

Leading the pack is **Stereophonic**, David Adjmi's meticulously crafted drama about a 1970s rock band in the studio. With 22 reviews and an 88/100 score, critics consistently praise its authentic portrayal of the creative process and its theatrical ambition. The production has established itself as one of the defining dramatic works of recent Broadway seasons.

Musical theater innovation shines through **Maybe Happy Ending**, which critics hail as one of Broadway's most original musicals in years. This charming robot love story, scoring 85/100 across 34 reviews, demonstrates that emotional depth and imaginative storytelling can coexist in unexpected narratives.

On the comedy front, **Oh, Mary!** has become a breakout sensation, with Cole Escola's irreverent take on Mary Todd Lincoln as a boozy, cabaret-obsessed narcissist earning raves for its riotous humor and Escola's fearless performance. The show's absurdist approach has resonated strongly with both critics and audiences.

The season also features strong revivals, including George C. Wolfe's reimagined **Gypsy** starring Audra McDonald and a lavish new production of **Oliver!**, alongside intimate dramas like **Mary Jane** and the dance-forward **Illinoise**.

Whether you're drawn to character-driven drama, musical innovation, or sharp comedy, these 2024 productions offer compelling reasons to experience Broadway's continued artistic vitality.

The season also showcases ambitious new American plays, including Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer-winning **English** (82/100), which explores language and identity with intelligence and sensitivity, and Branden Jacobs-Jenkins' **Purpose** (82/100), another sharp family drama from one of contemporary theater's most vital voices. Whether you're drawn to reimagined classics or bold new voices, this season's offerings provide compelling reasons to experience live theater at its finest.
